messages.subject: straight predictions from sampler
parts:
The help file for inla.posterior.sample provides the following toy example:

```
 set.seed(1234)
 n = 25
 xx = rnorm(n)
 yy = rev(xx)
 z = runif(n)
 y = rnorm(n)
 r = inla(y ~ 1 + z + f(xx) + f(yy, copy="xx"),
         data = data.frame(y, z, xx, yy), 
         control.compute = list(config=TRUE),
         family = "gaussian")
 x = inla.posterior.sample(100, r)
 
 fun = function(...) {
     mean(xx) - mean(yy)
 }
 f1 = inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, x)
```

Let's say we just wanted straight predictions of all (or even some) of the model components to new data (essentially, to compose a posterior predictive distribution of sorts).  Would the correct supplied function to inla.posterior.sample.eval just repeat some version of the original formula, e.g., "1 + z + xx + yy"?  I note that when I do this, I get columns for each sample but rows labeled "fun1" through "fun10."  I only get 1 row for each sample when take the mean as in the example above, but it's not entirely clear to me what this is the mean of or if this is desirable for my stated goal.

In the end, I'd like to have an equivalent of a posterior predictive distribution from which I can take the usual quantiles and such.

Appreciate any insight you have, and thanks very much for this interesting function.

Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] straight predictions from sampler
parts:
If you want to predict a new observation from the fitted model, you can
do as follows:


set.seed(1234)
n = 100
alpha = 1
beta = 1
s = 1
z = rnorm(n)
y = alpha + beta * z + rnorm(n, sd = s)
r = inla(y ~ 1 + z,
data = data.frame(y, z),

x = inla.posterior.sample(10^4, r)

znew = rnorm(1)
fun = function(zz = NA) {
return (Intercept + z * zz + rnorm(length(zz),
sd = sqrt(1/theta[1])))
}

f1 = inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, x, zz = znew)
hist(f1[1, ], n = 100, prob = TRUE)
m = alpha + beta * znew
xx = seq(m-4*s, m+4*s, by = s/100)
lines(xx, dnorm(xx, mean=m, sd = s), lwd=2)

which compares the posterior distribution from a new observation with
the one found from the fitted model.

Note that you need to know what 'theta' is, as its for the function
'fun', its only known as a vector.

inla.posterior.sample(), will by default, return samples of 'theta's in
the original parameterisation, meaning here, the precision. see the
help page.

you can also let 'znew' be a vector, for which you do this for several
new locations.

hope this helps.

H

PS: You can also process the output of posterior sample yourself, if
you rather want to, rather than using the '.fun' function.
